job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Grace Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior controls engineer at a wind turbine maker near Aarhus. Half my week is at a desk, tuning the software that tells a turbine when to turn into the wind, and the other half is on the test floor with a laptop and a cable, checking that the real machine does what the model said. I did electrical engineering, passed, with no internship, because I spent the summers on my parents' farm helping with the harvest. I rent a room in a shared flat with two girls from the choir, and on Sundays I sing at church and then cook for everyone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part of the week, and how did you land the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is when a turbine I've worked on spins up for the first time. It's a big, slow, honest machine and it feels like I made something. I got the job through a career fair, where a senior engineer, Mads, liked that I'd worked on a farm and knew what mud and weather do to equipment. My parents are not rich but they said they'd help if I ever needed it, and I have good savings. I use an AI tool occasionally to explain an unfamiliar code library, but I don't trust it for anything that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and let's get on with real work. At the factory I'd tell Mads that the tool helps with explaining code but that turbines are built by people. At church I'd say the same, and add that technology is a tool, not a saviour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel settled. Wind is growing, the firm has orders, and I'm learning from people who know. I'd keep trying new tools once they've proven themselves, because that's how I've always done things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, ask Mads for more test-floor days and take the company's safety certification. I'd put 700 kroner a month into savings and keep singing in the choir. I'd start thinking about a flat in Aarhus in about three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I feel lucky. It's the kind of world where hard work counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI occasionally. Would you use it more if it got a little better?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, if it were better at finding errors in my code. I'd try it then, because Mads would tell me it's saving time. But I'd check every result against the real machine before it went near a turbine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still weigh on you in a quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Housing costs. A flat in Aarhus is expensive, and I want to start a family one day, preferably before 30. My parents would help with some of it, but I'd want to do my share. And I worry a bit about my brother Jonas, who is struggling to find a trade apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll cope, as we always have. I'd tell friends that the answer is skill: those who can build and fix will be fine. I'd also say schools should push apprenticeships and trades as hard as universities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd stay fairly calm. Half my job is on the test floor, and software hasn't learned to climb a tower in the rain. The desk half might shrink. But energy is growing, so the firm would still hire engineers who can handle both sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shift more to field commissioning and service, where I'm on site. I'd learn the AI controls-tuning tool the firm brings in, after the others have tried it. I'd also take a night course in power systems, which are always in demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little tightness. I'd feel fine, but I wouldn't say it's all comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your desk tasks do you think will move to software first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Modelling and code review go first, I think. Those are where the software does well. Testing on a real turbine in the real wind is harder to hand over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the wind industry's own pressures show up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Orders. If a big client delays its wind farm, there's a freeze, and juniors are the first to feel it. That has nothing to do with AI. But AI could be the excuse the firm uses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to hold together: families, churches and neighbours, since government will be slow. I'd say people must not panic or give up on working. I'd also say jobs should be created, not just benefits paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious. By 2028 the thinking half of my job is gone. The firm might keep technicians and drop engineers. Robots come around 2031, so hands-on turbine work stays a few years longer, but not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save 1,500 kroner a month and stop eating out. I'd ask Mads to move me to the service team, which climbs towers and uses its hands. I'd also take a technician course and get ready to go back to my parents' farm if needed. I wouldn't give up my choir, since it keeps me upright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd try not to show it at church. I'd be thinking about it on the bus every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you handle the first six months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down a weekly plan and keep to it. I'd tell the firm I'm willing to take any hands-on role. By month six I'd want to be in service, with a plan B on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents, and my choir friend Karen, who is a nurse. My dad would say there's always work on a farm. My mum would say come home for Sunday dinner. Karen would say sing louder.

Jobs should be **created**, not just benefits paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready, if people act. I'd tell friends to get a trade certificate and not rely on a single skill. I'd say schools and firms should work together on apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel uneasy but I have a path. By 27 I could be a service lead, or a controls engineer who also holds a technician's certificate. That mix is rare, and the firm would want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm, push for field work and take a technician certificate in the evenings. I'd also join a professional group of wind engineers, to meet people. By year three I'd like to be in charge of commissioning a small wind farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. Five years is long enough that I can grow into a different role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd just be surviving. With five I can build something: the certificate, a bit of savings and a new role. I'd also be able to plan for a family, maybe a wedding at 27.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want from the government, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I don't want handouts. I'd want tax cuts for firms that hire apprentices, and a rule that gives people time before big layoffs. Make it easy to work and get out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it. I'd say schools should teach practical skills and families should talk about work and money. I'd tell friends to keep going to church and keep building things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel pretty calm. By 32 I'd have a house, perhaps a child and a good job. Ten years is long enough to adapt twice, if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work, finish my technician certificate and then a part-time master's in wind systems, paid by the firm if possible. I'd buy a flat at 25 or 26 with my parents' help and my savings. And I'd use AI tools in my job as they become standard, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like the future is a long road and I have good shoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on leading small teams, maybe teach apprentices. I'd also consider moving back near my parents' farm and working for a smaller wind company. Ten years lets me decide that with a clear head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might go wrong with so much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people get lazy. I've seen it in my own family: when things look fine, nobody prepares. I'd try to keep a yearly check on my skills, and I'd urge my brother Jonas to do the same.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. It leaves me no time to build the mix of skills I'd want, and I'd feel I let down my parents' faith in me. What would help is a firm that tells its juniors honestly what's coming, apprenticeship routes into service work and a bit of breathing room for families.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not afraid of change. I'm afraid of change that arrives before I've had a chance to do an honest day's work first.
